---
title: "Sorting Lists"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with Lists"
---

Python has built-in functions to find the largest and smallest values in a
list, and to put a list in order.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* find the largest and smallest value with `max()` and `min()`
* sort a list of strings or numbers, in either order
* find the top few values by sorting and slicing

**`max()` and `min()` return one element of a list. `sorted()` returns a new
list with all the elements in order, and leaves the original list unchanged.**

## Largest and smallest

This list has the annual rainfall in Bangalore, in millimetres, for each year
from 2016 to 2025:

```{python}
rainfall = [791, 1696, 618, 960, 1213, 1511, 1958, 1020, 1154, 1045]
```

The figures are measured by the India Meteorological Department (IMD), rounded
to whole millimetres. They come from the
[Bengaluru rainfall dataset](https://data.opencity.in/dataset/bengaluru-rainfall)
published by OpenCity.

The built-in `max()` function returns the largest element of a list:

```{python}
max(rainfall)
```

The `min()` function returns the smallest element:

```{python}
min(rainfall)
```

`max()` and `min()` work with a list of strings too. The largest string is the
one that comes last in alphabetical order, and the smallest is the one that
comes first:

```{python}
fruits = ["mango", "apple", "cherry", "banana"]
max(fruits)
```

```{python}
min(fruits)
```

## Sorting strings

The `sorted()` function takes a list as its argument and returns a new list
with the elements in order. A list of strings is sorted in alphabetical order:

```{python}
sorted(fruits)
```

Python compares strings one character at a time, from the first character. All
uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters, so a capitalised word
comes first:

```{python}
sorted(["banana", "Cherry", "apple"])
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Numbers stored as strings

Strings are compared character by character, even when they contain digits.
`"100"` comes before `"25"` because its first character, `"1"`, comes before
`"2"`:

```{python}
sorted(["10", "9", "100", "25"])
```

There is no error. The list is sorted, but not in numerical order. Convert the
strings to integers before sorting them as numbers.
:::

## Sorting numbers

A list of numbers is sorted from lowest to highest:

```{python}
sorted(rainfall)
```

The returned list is a new list. `rainfall` still has its original order:

```{python}
rainfall
```

To keep the sorted list, assign it to a variable:

```{python}
sorted_rainfall = sorted(rainfall)
sorted_rainfall
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The `sort()` method

Lists also have a `sort()` method. Unlike `sorted()`, it does not return a new
list. It changes the list itself, so the original order is lost. Prefer
`sorted()` over the `sort()` method.

This is how the `sort()` method changes a list:

```{python}
scores = [72, 95, 64]
scores.sort()
scores
```
:::

## Sorting in reverse

`sorted()` accepts a second argument, `reverse=True`, to sort from highest to
lowest:

```{python}
sorted(rainfall, reverse=True)
```

`reverse=True` is a **keyword argument**: an argument passed with a name. The
name says what the value means, which a plain `True` would not.

## The top few values

`max()` gives only the highest value. For the two highest rainfall figures,
sort the list in reverse and slice the first two elements:

```{python}
sorted(rainfall, reverse=True)[:2]
```

For the two lowest rainfall figures, sort the list from lowest to highest and
slice the first two elements:

```{python}
sorted(rainfall)[:2]
```

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `max(rainfall)` | returns the largest element |
| `min(rainfall)` | returns the smallest element |
| `max(fruits)` | returns the string that comes last in alphabetical order |
| `sorted(fruits)` | returns a new list of strings in alphabetical order |
| `sorted(rainfall)` | returns a new list of numbers from lowest to highest |
| `sorted(rainfall, reverse=True)` | returns a new list from highest to lowest |
| `reverse=True` | a keyword argument: an argument passed with a name |
| `sorted(rainfall, reverse=True)[:2]` | the two highest values |
| `sorted(rainfall)[:2]` | the two lowest values |
| sorting strings | uppercase letters come before lowercase letters |
| sorting strings of digits | compares characters, so `"100"` comes before `"25"` |
| `sorted()` | leaves the original list unchanged |
| `scores.sort()` | sorts `scores` in place and changes it; prefer `sorted()` |

And the one idea to carry forward: use `max()` or `min()` for one value, and
`sorted()` with a slice for the top or bottom few. `sorted()` returns a new
list and leaves the original list as it was.
